newsitem.title: GERMANY: Opinion - German Jobs not secure employment.
newsitem.headline: Opinion - German Jobs not secure employment.

text.p: By Dr Heinz Grimm, senior economist at Bankgesellschaft

At the beginning of the year unemployment in Germany hit a dismal record: 4.658 million officially registered unemployed with an estimated unregistered two million in short-time work, job creation, retraining schemes or early retirement.

Even if an increase in the unemployment figures was to be expected at the beginning of the year due to seasonal factors, the extent of the rise is alarming. Once the unemployment figures have been adjusted to take account of the seasonal components, in January economic reasons alone accounted for about 160,000 additional unemployed. This unexpectedly high increase in unemployment demands immediate action.

The budget risks - an increase in unemployment benefit payments on the one hand and a decrease in tax income on the other - connected with the achievement of the Maastricht debt criteria have pushed employment policy to the political fore. At least there is broad consensus as to the causes of unemployment: a too rapid increase in wage costs, too narrow wage spread, too high social security and tax deductions, state overregulation and outdated structures and inflexibility in both the public and private sectors of the economy.

In order to solve the problem of unemployment, we need to say goodbye to the old way of thinking based on 'vested rights' - and that is where the crux of the problem lies. The proposal has been made that a solution should be sought at round-table talks to which all interested parties should contribute. This populist strategy is, however, doomed to failure as not all the interested parties will be represented at the negotiating table. The result is bound to be slight cosmetic changes and not a radical change of course.

The losers within current economic policy are hardly likely to be represented: entrepreneurs who due to overregulation have not had the chance to bring new and/or more intelligent products on the market, and who thus would represent competition for established companies. The employees who would have found a job in such promising new companies will naturally also be excluded from the negotiating table, in the same way as the unemployed who have lost their jobs as a result of wage cost-induced rationalisation efforts.

Potential entrepreneurs and employees in desirable service industries, who are replaced by internal solutions due to the exorbitant discrepancy between high prices caused by tax and social security contributions and low net purchasing power, are kept from the negotiating table in the same way as black market representatives, those who do not want simply to stand by and watch in the face of this discrepancy and who by breaking the law create employment and income which would otherwise be lost to the community.

On the contrary, the interest groups who will be present at the round-table will be more or less uniformly those who have profited the most from economic policy up until now, and who will therefore show little interest in a change in the status quo.

It will only be possible to implement changes in employment policy successfully once the general awareness has been heightened to the point where the associated political pressure becomes so strong that radical political changes are made.

This change in awareness has to set in in those areas where previously the mind-set was focused on concepts such as secure employment or long-term employment relationships: it is not a question of the preservation of employment or maintenance of the employment relationship at all costs -- even in the case where the cost is ever increasing unemployment. The point is that every individual should have a job to do, providing a service at a price which society is prepared to pay. That goes for the private sector of the economy as well as for the state sector.

If the service is not worth the money, it will have to be taken off the market. Only in this way can the constant incentive to continually improve one's own performance be achieved. The preservation of employment, whether by means of protection against dismissal or through subsidies, which means financing services which do not have a sufficient market value, leads nowhere.
Preventing an exit from the market has as a price the manifold prevention of others entering the market. The consequence is the gradual impoverishment of society and a loss of solidarity.

Only a performance- or job-orientated society can create the wealth needed to generate sufficient strength to help individuals to help themselves. "Job"-thinking is required, not the thinking governed by the attitude that everybody has a right to employment which leads to the paralysis and eventually to the decline of the economy.
